# Mining Correlated Motifs with Wildcards in PPI Networks: Exact and Optimal

Lucas P. Oliveira<sup>∗</sup> Ben Bals<sup>†</sup> Aalt D. J. van Dijk<sup>‡</sup> Solon P. Pissis§

**Abstract.** A _protein-protein interaction_ (PPI) network is a graph whose nodes are protein sequences and whose edges represent physical interactions between proteins. _Correlated Motif Mining_ (CMM) seeks pairs of sequence motifs whose co-occurrence in interacting proteins reveals binding sites and interaction mechanisms. Formally, in the \((\ell,d)\)-CMM problem, we are given a graph _G_=(_V,E_), with \(V\subseteq\Sigma^*\) for an alphabet \(\Sigma\), and integers \(0\le d<\ell\), and we seek a pair {_X,Y_} of motifs, each of length \(\ell\) and containing _d_ wildcards, that maximizes a support measure _f(G,{X,Y_}); e.g., the count _f<sub>E</sub>_ of edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\) such that _X_ matches a substring of _u_ and _Y_ matches a substring of _v_, or vice versa. Although existing approaches have produced biologically meaningful results, they are either inefficient or heuristic-based, as the underlying optimization problem is NP-hard. Here, we revisit \((\ell,d)\)-CMM. For _d_=0, we give an exact O(_N_<sup>2</sup>)-time and O(_N_)-space algorithm, where _N_ is the total length of the node strings, and prove that this time is conditionally optimal under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis. For any _d\>_0, we give an exact \(\mathcal{O}\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2N^2\right)\)-time and O(_N_)-space algorithm, and observe that the problem is W[1]-hard parameterized by _d_. The latter algorithm improves the state of the art by exponentially large factors in both time and space. We further demonstrate experimentally that our algorithms are practical on real-world PPI networks and find significantly higher-scoring motif pairs than the state of the art. Moreover, we show that our algorithms find many top-scoring motif pairs that the state of the art misses entirely. Taken together, our results suggest that exact CMM with wildcards is more tractable in practice than previously assumed.

**1 Introduction.** Large-scale biological networks capturing protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are now available for a wide range of organisms [20-22]. While such data reveal how proteins function within a PPI

network, they offer no direct insight into how those interactions are encoded at the sequence level--in particular, which regions of protein sequences correspond to physical interaction sites. Popular tools such as AlphaFold [11] have revolutionized protein structure prediction, but experimental validation of interaction interfaces at scale remains a major bottleneck: the human proteome alone contains tens of thousands of binary interactions [20], and determining their structural basis experimentally is infeasible at this scale. Moreover, even large-scale structural characterization of interacting proteins would not directly answer the question of how interaction specificity is encoded in protein sequence or structure. In other words: _which specific residues determine which partners a protein can bind?_

To answer this question, a variety of bioinformatics approaches have been developed [8,10,23]. In particular, several algorithmic approaches have been proposed for locating binding sites by mining overrepresented pairs of sequence patterns, called _motif pairs_, from sequences of interacting proteins [1,15-18,25]. One such approach, known as _Correlated Motif Mining_ (CMM), identifies binding sites by searching for a consensus pattern in one group of proteins that interacts with nearly all proteins containing a second consensus pattern. When such a pair is found, both patterns are likely to represent complementary surface regions that enable physical binding. Figure 1.1 illustrates this idea: \(\{\mathsf{G}\diamond\mathsf{P}\diamond\mathsf{NY},\mathsf{P}\diamond\mathsf{P}\}\) and \(\{\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{pS},\mathsf{L}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{pS}\}\) are two correlated motif pairs, where an undirected edge connects two protein sequences if the first contains motif \(\mathsf{G}\diamond\mathsf{P}\diamond\mathsf{NY}\) and the second contains motif \(\mathsf{P}\diamond\mathsf{P}\), and analogously for \(\{\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{pS},\mathsf{L}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{pS}\}\). Although it remains unclear what fraction of protein interfaces can be described by correlated motifs of this kind, existing approaches consistently show that such motifs do contain meaningful information about interaction interfaces.

Existing computational approaches fall into two broad categories: (i) interaction-driven approaches [16-18]; and (ii) motif-driven approaches [1, 15,25]. Interaction-driven approaches search for (quasi- )bicliques--that is, subsets of nodes in a PPI network, in which nearly every node on one side is connected to nearly all nodes on the other. These subgraphs capture an all-versus-all, or most-versus-most, interaction

Motif- driven approaches, by contrast, begin with candidate motif pairs and evaluate their support directly in the PPI network. While both paradigms have been shown to yield biologically meaningful results, the motif-driven approach has several conceptual advantages over its interaction-driven counterpart. First, motif pairs are identified directly rather than derived in post-processing. Second, all proteins containing a given motif are taken into account, rather than an arbitrarily selected subset. Third, when the interactions between two groups of proteins arise from multiple compatible binding sites--e.g., \(\{\mathsf{G}\diamond\diamond\mathsf{P}\diamond\mathsf{NY},\mathsf{P}\diamond\diamond\mathsf{P}\}\) and \(\{\mathsf{R}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\diamond\mathsf{pS},\mathsf{L}\diamond\mathsf{R}\diamond\diamond\mathsf{pS}\}\) in Figure 1.1-- interaction-driven methods are forced to merge them into one motif pair, thereby losing this structural distinction.

## 1.1 The problem and the state of the art.

In this paper, we focus on the motif-driven approach to CMM. The vanilla version of the problem is defined as follows.

We next define the CMM problem _with wildcards_; wildcards are placeholder symbols, denoted by \(\diamond\), that can match any character from the underlying alphabet.

While we formalize the problems in a general form, the motivating application leads us to use the following widely-used support measures \[1,15,25\]: the count _f<sub>E</sub>_ of edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\) such that _X_ matches a substring of _u_<tbc>

<tbc>and _Y_ matches a substring of _v_, or vice versa; and the \(\chi^2\)-score \(f_{\chi^2}\) of _G_ with respect to {_X,Y_} \[25\].

To the best of our knowledge, three techniques have so far been proposed. Unfortunately, these techniques differ not only in their mining method, but also in the matching relation and the support measure used.

The first work by Tan et al. \[25\] introduced D- MOTIF, an exact algorithm for finding correlated motif pairs under the Hamming distance. D-MOTIF considers \(f_{\chi^2}\) to quantify support. The basic idea of the algorithm is to enumerate all possible motif pairs from every pair \(\{u,v\}\in E\), using the _Hamming distance neighborhood_ notion, and then check if they have enough support. The authors also suggested a heuristic counterpart called D- STAR. Unfortunately, neither D-MOTIF nor D-STAR scales to networks with more than 250 proteins.

The second work by Leung et al. \[15\] introduced FindMotif, an exact algorithm for \((\ell,d)\)-CMM. FindMotif uses a different support measure that considers the probability that the observed number of interactions is generated under a null hypothesis. The algorithm builds a table of \(\mathcal{O}(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2|\Sigma|^{2(\ell-d)})\) entries, one per possible motif pair over alphabet \(\Sigma\), and computes the support for each using a _voting_ technique. The authors also suggested a heuristic counterpart called MotifHeuristics, which was able to handle larger networks than D-STAR.

The third work by Boyen et al. \[1\] proved that \((\ell,d)\)-CMM is NP-hard for so-called _compliant bicliquemaximal_ measures, which include _f<sub>E</sub>_ and \(f_{\chi^2}\). They also introduced SLIDER, a generic metaheuristic that incorporates two _steepest-ascent_ procedures. The central component of these procedures is a neighborhood function defined by viewing a motif as a window that slides along the protein sequence of one of the proteins. Unlike more conventional neighborhood functions, this has a clear biological interpretation: if a motif partially overlaps a binding site in a sequence, a few mutations should suffice to convert it into a binding site. In this sense, both neighborhood functions are designed to identify nearby motifs that may correspond to regions close to one another on actual proteins. The difference is that one neighborhood function considers as neighbors all motifs that could, in principle, lie near the given motif on any protein, whereas the other restricts attention to motifs that are actually nearby on a single selected protein. Although SLIDER can be paired with an arbitrary support measure, the authors used \(f_{\chi^2}\), providing compelling evidence that it is biologically the most relevant, and showing that SLIDER outperforms MotifHeuristics.

Consequently, the main aim of the existing works \[1, 15, 25\] has been to design efficient and effective _heuristics_ that identify high-quality motif pairs in reasonable time. This need is particularly acute for modern real-world datasets, which are large, noisy, and in need of methods that scale while still capturing biologically meaningful patterns.

Here, however, we present an _exact_ method that remains efficient in practice on modern datasets, thereby showing that the problem can be solved far more effectively than is commonly believed. Our results thus refute the prevailing view that only heuristic approaches are viable for this task. Our crucial observation is that the hardness proof in \[1\] proceeds under the assumption that both \(\ell\) and _d_ are unbounded, which is not realistic in the motivating application. Intuitively, we confine the computational hardness to _parameter_ \(\ell\). Indeed, the values considered for \(\ell\) and _d_ are typically small \[1, 15, 25\].

We make the following theoretical contributions:

(1) We give an _exact_ O(_N_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithm for CMM (the vanilla version), where \(N:=\sum_{v\in V}|v|\). The space usage is O(_N_). See Section 3.<tbc>

(3) We build on the CMM algorithm to give an _exact_ \(\mathcal{O}\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2N^2\right)\)-time algorithm for \((\ell,d)\)-CMM (the wildcards version). This improves dramatically on the state of the art from \(\mathcal{O}^*\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2|\Sigma|^{2(\ell-d)}\right)\) time to \(\mathcal{O}^*\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2\right)\) and from \(\mathcal{O}^*\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2|\Sigma|^{2(\ell-d)}\right)\) space to O(_N_).<sup>1</sup> See Section 4.<tbc>

We make the following practical contributions:

(1) We show that the parallelized version of our algorithm for \((\ell,d)\)-CMM processes real-world datasets in a reasonable amount of time.<tbc>

(2) We show that the runtime and space usage predicted by our theoretical results are accurately reflected in practice.<tbc>

(3) We show that our exact algorithm finds motif pairs with significantly higher support than the state of the art, which highlights its usefulness.<tbc>

(4) We show that our exact algorithm finds many top- scoring motif pairs that the state of the art misses.<tbc>

## 2 Preliminaries.

We assume throughout that arrays and strings start at position 1.

### 2.1 Strings.

A _string_ is a finite sequence of characters over an alphabet \(\Sigma\). In this work, we consider strings over a totally ordered alphabet. We denote the length of a string _T_ by |_T_|. For any index \(i\in[1,|T|]\), we denote the _i_-th character of _T_ by _T_\[_i_\]. A string of the form \(T[i..j]=T[i]T[i+1]\cdots T[j]\), where \(1\le i\le j\le|T|\), is called a _fragment_ of _T_. If _T_ is known, we can encode _T_\[_i..j_\] in O(1) space as the pair (_i,j_). A fragment of the form _T_\[1_..j_\] is called a _prefix_ of _T_, and a fragment of the form _T_\[_i.._|_T_\] is called a _suffix_ of _T_. A string _P_ is a _substring_ of _T_ if _P=T_\[_i..i_+|_P_|-1\], for some _i_. In this case, we say that _P occurs_ in _T_. A _wildcard_ is a special symbol \(\diamond\) matching any \(a\in\Sigma\sqcup\{\diamond\}\).

Given a string _T_ of length _n_, the _suffix array_ of _T_, denoted by SA_<sub>T</sub>_\[1_..n_\], stores a permutation of the indices {1_,...,n_} such that _T_\[SA_<sub>T</sub>_\[_i\..n_\] is the _i_-th lexicographically smallest suffix of _T_. Let lcp(_X,Y_) denote the length of the _longest common prefix_ (LCP) of the strings _X_ and _Y_ . The _LCP array_ of _T_, denoted by LCP_<sub>T</sub>_\[1_..n_\], is defined as follows: LCP_<sub>T</sub>_\[1\]=0, and for every \(i\in[2,n]\), \(\text{LCP}_T[i]=\mathrm{lcp}\left(T[\text{SA}_T[i-1]\dots n],T[\text{SA}_T[i]\dots n]\right)\).

### 2.2 Graphs and motifs.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be an undirected graph, where \(V\subseteq\Sigma^*\), for an alphabet \(\Sigma\). Let \(N:=\sum_{v\in V}|v|\) denote the total length of all \(v\in V\) . An \((\ell,d)\)_-motif_ is a string \(X\in(\Sigma\sqcup\{\diamond\})^\ell\) containing exactly _d_ wildcard symbols \(\diamond\). When _d_=0, the motif is simply a string over \(\Sigma\) of length \(\ell\). An \((\ell,d)\)_-motif pair_ {_X,Y_} is an unordered pair of \((\ell,d)\)-motifs. We may omit \(\ell\) and _d_ when they are clear from the context and then simply speak of motifs and motif pairs.

### 2.3 Motif-induced subgraphs.

For a motif _X_, let \(V_X:=\{v\in V|X\text{occurs in}v\}\) be the set of nodes where _X_ occurs. If a node _v_ contains multiple occurrences of _X_, then _v_ is included only once in _V<sub>X</sub>_.

For a motif pair {_X,Y_}, the set of edges whose endpoints contain _X_ and _Y_ , respectively, is

\(E_{X,Y}:=\{\{u,v\}\in E|u\in V_X\text{and}v\in V_Y\}.\)

We set _f<sub>E</sub>(G,{X,Y_}):=|_E<sub>X,Y</sub>_|. The subgraph _selected_ by {_X,Y_} is then \(G_{X,Y}:=(V_X\cup V_Y,E_{X,Y})\). If \(V_X\cap V_Y\) is nonempty, we may have an edge between distinct nodes \(v,u\in V_X\) provided that at least one of them is in \(V_X\cap V_Y\). On the other hand, if \(v,u\in V_X\backslash V_Y\), they cannot be adjacent by definition of _E<sub>X,Y</sub>_.

A motif pair {_X,Y_} is called a (_k<sub>X</sub>,k<sub>Y</sub>,k<sub>X,Y</sub>)-motif pair_ for _G_ if _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_ satisfies |_V<sub>X</sub>_|=_k<sub>X</sub>_, |_V<sub>Y</sub>_|=_k<sub>Y</sub>_, and<tbc>

\(|V_X\cap V_Y|=k_{X,Y}\). It is called _complete_ if every node of _V<sub>X</sub>_ is adjacent to every node of _V<sub>Y</sub>_. A complete bipartite graph is called a _biclique_.

**2.4 Support measures.** A _support measure f_ on _G_ is a function that maps an \((\ell,d)\)-motif pair {_X,Y_} to a nonnegative real number _f(G,{X,Y_}). Different types of support functions have been considered in the literature \[1,15,25\]. We restrict our attention to _f<sub>E</sub>_ and \(f_{\chi^2}\), which we define below. The former is simple and illustrative and will serve to make our theoretical analysis lucid. The second works well in practice \[1\] and we use it in our experimental evaluation (we also show that our theoretical results extend to it).

**2.5 The** \(f_{\chi^2}\) **support measure.** The \(\chi^2\)-based support measure of a graph _G_ with respect to an \((\ell,d)\)- motif pair {_X,Y_}, denoted by \(f_{\chi^2}\), is defined as<tbc>

\(f_{\chi^2}(G,\{X,Y\}):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\frac{(|E_{X,Y}|-\overline{E_{X,Y}})^2}{\overline{E_{X,Y}}} & \text{if}|E_{X,Y}|>\overline{E_{X,Y}}, \\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>where <o>_E<sub>X,Y</sub>_</o> is the expected number of edges between _V<sub>X</sub>_ and _V<sub>Y</sub>_ under a uniform random-graph model. Concretely,<tbc>

\(\overline{E_{X,Y}}:=\text{ed}(G)\cdot E_{k_X,k_Y,k_{X,Y}}^\mathrm{max},\)

<tbc>where \(\text{ed}(G):=|E|/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{|V|}{2}\) is the _edge density_ of _G_, and

\(E_{k_X,k_Y,k_{X,Y}}^\mathrm{max}:=k_Xk_Y-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k_{X,Y}}{2}-k_{X,Y}\)

is the maximum possible number of edges in the subgraph selected by any (_k<sub>X</sub>,k<sub>Y</sub>,k<sub>X,Y</sub>_)-motif pair. The parameters _k<sub>X</sub>_, _k<sub>Y</sub>_, and _k<sub>X,Y</sub>_ are as defined above; |_V_| and |_E_| are trivially obtained from the input. Intuitively, this measure captures how much above the average density a subgraph selected by a motif pair is, taking into account its size.

**3 An exact algorithm for CMM.** To simplify our presentation, we focus on the _f<sub>E</sub>_ support measure for now, but the same algorithmic ideas also apply to the \(f_{\chi^2}\) support measure. Recall that _f<sub>E</sub>(G,{X,Y_}) counts the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\) such that _X_ matches a substring of _u_ and _Y_ matches a substring of _v_, or vice versa.

Theorem 3.1. _There is an algorithm for CMM with f<sub>E</sub> running in time_ O(_N_<sup>2</sup>)_, where_ \(N:=\sum_{v\in V}|v|\)_. The space used is_ O(_N)._

_Proof._ The algorithm (see Algorithm 3.1) iterates over all motif pairs {_X,Y_}, such that _X_ and _Y_ are substrings of at least one of the labels, and then counts the corresponding number of edges. That is, it computes<tbc>

<tbc>the value _f<sub>E</sub>(G,{X,Y_}) explicitly. Therefore, taking the maximum will clearly produce the desired output.

The more interesting part is how to implement some of the operations efficiently enough. The short version is that the suffix array (SA) will give us all the necessary tools. First, observe that we can construct the SA of the concatenation of the node strings (with some separation character) in O(_N_) time \[12\] after sorting all characters occurring in all strings \(v\in V\) in O(_N_log_N_) time. The SA (together with the LCP array) gives us a constant- size unique name for each length-\(\ell\) substring of any label that can be computed (after preprocessing) in constant time given a location in a node string. Call this the _rank_ of a substring. Note that the ranks are the same for all occurrences of the same substring. In addition, these are integers bounded by _N_. One may think of this as a perfect hash function that we can use to (1) compare substrings in constant time, and (2) implement the dictionary _C_ defined in Line 1 using O(_N_) space. Using (1) and (2), we implement the loop in Line 3 so that it runs in O(_N_) time. In particular, after a single linear pass over the node strings, we use these names to build a simple inverse index to access the nodes that contain a given rank, as required in Line 4. As we access the nodes for each label exactly once and this inverse index has total size O(_N_), that is also the total time to access the nodes. Similarly, observe that in a linear pass, we can build a list of the unique ranks that occur in each node, making the loop in Line 6 take O(_N_) time in total for each _X_. The operations in the innermost loop require constant time. In particular, the operation \(\unknown\) can be any total order on the length-\(\ell\) substrings. To get a constant-time comparator, we choose the rank order.

Thus, we are finally left to argue why the loop in Line 5 does not blow up the running time. Observe that each edge {_u,v_} is only considered for a motif pair {_X,Y_} if _X_ occurs in _u_ and _Y_ occurs in _v_. (Each edge is visited exactly once in Line 5, oriented so that \(u\in V_X\); the second loop adds the _Y_ ’s that occur only in _u_.) This can happen at most \((|u|-\ell+1)(|v|-\ell+1)\) times. Then

\(\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}(|u|-\ell+1)(|v|-\ell+1)\le\sum_{(u,v)\in V\times V}|u||v|=\left(\sum_{u\in V}|u|\right)\left(\sum_{v\in V}|v|\right)=\mathcal{O}(N^2),\)

yields the desired bound. The space used is O(_N_) as SA and _C_ are implemented in O(_N_) space. \(\sqcap\sqcup\)

We defer the changes required for \(f_{\chi^2}\) and the SETH lower bounds for both _fE_ and \(f_{\chi^2}\) to Appendix A. ## 4 An exact algorithm for \((\ell,d)\)-CMM. Algorithm 3.1 for CMM (Theorem 3.1) will serve as a basis for our exact algorithm for \((\ell,d)\)-CMM. The basic premise is simple: iterate over all possible combinations of wildcard positions in the two motifs and then run a modified version of Algorithm 3.1 that ignores the characters at these positions. While this seems easy, achieving it without losing efficiency is somewhat tricky, especially when targeting O(_N_) space. Recall that in Algorithm 3.1, we heavily relied on the rank of every length-\(\ell\) substring in the suffix array (SA) of the concatenated node strings. In particular, we relied on the fact that this rank is a compact representation of the substrings. Thus, we were able to compare any two substrings for equality by simply comparing their ranks. With the _d_ wildcards, we need to treat substrings that are actually different as the same, that is, we have a relaxed notion of equality that ignores the wildcarded positions. Defining the right notion of rank and implementing access to it efficiently requires a substantial amount of care. We show the following core lemma. Lemma 4.1. _Given a set_ \(V\subseteq\Sigma^*\) _of strings of total length N over_ \(\Sigma=\{1,2,\dots,N\}\)_, an integer_ \(\ell\in[1,N]\)_, and a set_ \(H\subseteq[\ell]\) _with_ \(d:=|H|<\ell\)_, we can construct an_ O(_N)-size data structure in_ O((_d_+1)_N_) _time and_ O(_N_) _working space answering the following queries in_ O(1) _time: given_ (_u,i), with_ \(u\in V\) _and_ \(i\in[1,|u|-\ell+1]\)_, return a_ rank _(a unique identifier) of string M of length_ \(\ell\)_, such that, for all_ \(j\in[1,\ell]\): \(M[j]:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \diamond & \text{\textit{if}}j\in H, \\ u[i+j-1] & \text{\textit{if}}j\notin H. \end{array}\right.\) _In particular, the output rank is an integer from_ \[0_,N)._ _Proof._ Consider Algorithm 4.1. We show that this algorithm solves exactly the claimed task. Let \(H=\{h_1<\cdotsV_:=|_SV_|-|_V_|. (We will ignore suffixes of _SV_ starting with separators.) In O(_NV_) time, we construct the suffix array SA_SV_ \[12\] and the LCP array LCP_SV_ \[13\]. Consider the list of the suffixes of _SV_. The characters that occur at the positions _h_1_,...,hd_ of every suffix are replaced by wildcards to obtain _NV_ suffixes each split into (_d_+1) fragments. The above replacements are _implicit_; we never apply them. Moreover, we are interested only in the length-\(\ell\) prefix of each suffix. Some care is needed: if a suffix is shorter than \(\ell\), we ignore it from any further computation; and if a suffix contains a separator #_i_ in its length-\(\ell\) prefix, we also ignore it. Using SA_SV_ and starting with the first _NV_ substrings (prefixes of suffixes) of length exactly (_h_1-1), a new rank is assigned to each of them according to the lexicographical ordering of these substrings; this can be easily derived from a single scan of LCP_SV_ in O(_NV_) time. We then proceed to _h_2 analogously, and so on. To maintain O(_NV_) space, for every consecutively considered pair of wildcard positions, we use radix sort over the _NV_ pairs of ranks (corresponding to the _NV_ suffixes) to obtain a new integer ranking over \[0_,NV_), and the process continues. In the end, we have a new lexicographical ordering of the length-\(\ell\) prefixes of suffixes of _SV_ that disregards the characters at the _h_1- th_,...,hd_-th positions. Moreover, for every two successive length-\(\ell\) prefixes in this order, we know whether they

Since this list is sorted, identical length-\(\ell\) prefixes (here identical means with _d_ wildcards) are _grouped_ and so each group member gets the same rank from \[0_,NV_). Two length-\(\ell\) substrings are identical under _H_ if and only if their constituent fragments between the indices of _H_ are identical. By treating each substring as a tuple of ranks corresponding to these fragments--specifically (_r_1_,r_2_,...,r__d_+1)--and applying radix sort, we obtain a lexicographical ordering (of the suffixes) based strictly on the subsequence of non-wildcard characters. This correctly groups all occurrences of a specific motif _M_ into a contiguous range in the sorted list. The ranks (unique identifiers) are stored in the array R returned by Algorithm 4.1, indexed by the starting position of each suffix in _SV_. Given \(u\in V\) and an offset _i_, the length-\(\ell\) prefix of the corresponding suffix is exactly the length-\(\ell\) substring \(u[i..i+\ell-1]\); hence, a single lookup in R returns its identifier in O(1) time, which is invariant under replacing the positions in _H_ by \(\diamond\), as claimed. **4.1 Parallelization.** The algorithm of Theorem 4.3 is easy to parallelize since the computation can be carried out independently for each _wildcard combination_. As motif pairs are unordered, roughly half of the \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}^2\) combinations need to be considered, giving \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}+1\right)/2\) independent jobs, each running in O(_N_<sup>2</sup>) time. For \(H\neq H'\), the motifs _X_ and _Y_ are always distinct, so the tie-breaking test \(X\unknown Y\) of Algorithm 3.1 is applied only in the jobs with \(H=H'\). Since each thread processes a disjoint subset of the motif pairs, the global optimum is the maximum of the per-job optima, so aggregation is trivial. We will later see that this is both easy to implement and efficient in practice. Moreover, by using Theorem 4.3, O(_N_) space is used per thread.

**5 Experimental results.** In this section, we compare our exact algorithm against SEQ-SLIDER and M-SLIDER, two variants of SLIDER \[1\], the state-of- the-art (heuristic) method. Each employs a different neighborhood function when sliding over neighboring motifs during steepest ascent. We also empirically evaluate the time and space complexities of our exact algorithm to confirm our theoretical findings. These goals were split into the following research questions:

**RQ1:** How do the scores of SLIDER’s solution set compare to the ones of the optimal solution set?<tbc>

**RQ2:** What is the recall of SLIDER’s solution set relative to the optimal solution set?<tbc>

**RQ3:** How does our algorithm scale as |_V_| (and thus _N_) grows?<tbc>

**RQ4:** How does our algorithm scale as |_E_| grows?<tbc>

**RQ5:** How does our algorithm scale as the number _t_ of threads used increases?

In our evaluation, we used the more lenient version \(s_\ell\) for a motif length \(\ell\); that is, we afforded SLIDER’s solution set more slack when it was compared to our exact algorithm’s solution set.

_Reduced solution set._ Let _S_={_M_<sub>1</sub>_,M_<sub>2</sub>_,...,M<sub>k</sub>_} be a solution set ranked from the highest-scoring motif pair _M_<sub>1</sub> to the lowest-scoring one, _M<sub>k</sub>_. We construct a _reduced solution set_ \(S^*\subseteq S\) with the following property: for any distinct motif pairs \(M'\) and \(M''\) in _S_<sup>∗</sup>, we require that \(s_0(M',M'')<1\). Note that our similarity relation _s<sub>h</sub>_ is not transitive, so there may exist multiple subsets of _S_ with this property. Following the approach of \[1\], our set _S_<sup>∗</sup> is constructed with the following greedy strategy: for each _i_=1_,...,k_, we remove every \(M_j\in S\) with _j\>i_ satisfying _s_<sub>0</sub>(_M<sub>i</sub>,M<sub>j</sub>_)=1.

_Coverage of one solution set by another._ Given two reduced solution sets _S<sub>A</sub>_ and _S<sub>B</sub>_, we define the _coverage of S<sub>B</sub> by S<sub>A</sub>_, parameterized by _h_ and \(\tau\), as

\(\text{Cov}_{h,\tau,A}(S_B):=\frac{|\{M\in S_B|\exists M'\in S_A,s_h(M,M')\ge\tau\}|}{|S_B|}.\)

This resembles the notion of _recall_: we are effectively measuring the fraction of motif pairs from _S<sub>B</sub>_ retrieved by _A_ (under similarity _s<sub>h</sub>_ at a threshold \(\tau\)).

### A.1 The \(f_{\chi^2}\) support measure.

While the function _f<sub>E</sub>_ lends itself well to our theoretical analysis, it is not ideal for the biological domain. In particular, in a PPI network, maximizing the _f<sub>E</sub>_ function finds a motif pair {_X,Y_} that potentially explains many interactions (i.e., there are many edges where _X_ appears on one side and _Y_ on the other). To make it more likely we find an actual interaction, we also want the property that there are few _non_-edges where _X_ appears on one side and _Y_ on the other. In other words, we want the presence of _X_ and _Y_ to make an interaction likely. This is not captured by _f<sub>E</sub>_. In graph-theoretic terms, we want to ensure that the subgraph selected by {_X,Y_} is _dense_. Here, this means denser than the average over the whole interaction network. This is exactly what the \(f_{\chi^2}\) support function is designed to capture. Boyen et al. "experimentally establish the superiority of the Chi-square-based support measure over other support measures" \[1\].

Fortunately, the hard part in computing \(f_{\chi^2}\) turns out to be computing _f<sub>E</sub>_. In the following corollary, we show that the additional information needed to derive \(f_{\chi^2}(G,\{X,Y\})\) from _f<sub>E</sub>(G,{X,Y_})=|_E<sub>X,Y</sub>_| is easy to compute, lifting Algorithm 3.1 to support \(f_{\chi^2}\).

Corollary A.1 (to Theorem 3.1). _There is an algorithm for CMM with_ \(f_{\chi^2}\) _running in time_ O(_N_<sup>2</sup>)_, where_ \(N=\sum_{v\in V}|v|\)_. The space used is_ O(_N)._

_Proof._ We sketch how to adapt Algorithm 3.1. Given a graph _G_=(_V,E_), where \(V\subseteq\Sigma^*\), and a positive integer \(\ell\), our goal is to find a pair {_X,Y_} of motifs maximizing \(f_{\chi^2}(G,\{X,Y\})\). Computing this quantity reduces to computing the following parameters: the number _k<sub>X</sub>_ (resp. _k<sub>Y</sub>_) of nodes in which _X_ (resp. _Y_ ) occurs, the number _k<sub>X,Y</sub>_ of nodes in which both _X_ and _Y_ occur, and the number |_E<sub>X,Y</sub>_| of edges in which _X_ occurs in an endpoint and _Y_ occurs in the other.

The number |_E<sub>X,Y</sub>_| of edges can be easily obtained in O(_N_<sup>2</sup>) time using Theorem 3.1. For _k<sub>X</sub>_ (resp. _k<sub>Y</sub>_), iterate over the nodes and, for each distinct length-\(\ell\) substring _X_ of the current node, increment a counter indexed by rank(_X_). By handling duplicates locally at each node, this counting can be done in O(_N_) time. This is a simplification of Algorithm 3.1. Finally, for _k<sub>X,Y</sub>_, construct a graph \(G'\) from _G_ as follows. Let \(V(G')=V\) and \(E(G')=\{\{v,v\}|v\in V\}\). Applying Algorithm 3.1 to \(G'\) yields the desired number _k<sub>X,Y</sub>_ for every pair of length-\(\ell\) substrings {_X,Y_}. (Algorithm 3.1 and its analysis apply to graphs with self-loops). \(\sqcap\sqcup\)

## B Materials omitted from Section 4.

### B.1 Why we cannot hope for a running time polynomial in \(\ell\).

The result of Section 4 can be couched in parameterized complexity terms to say that \((\ell,d)\)- CMM is fixed-parameter tractable (in FPT) by \(\ell\) (since \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell}{d}\le 2^\ell\)). Since \(\ell\) is a larger parameter than _d_ (except in trivial instances), it is natural to ask if \((\ell,d)\)-CMM is in FPT by _d_, too. That is, whether there is an algorithm with a running time of the form \(\mathcal{O}(f(d)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(N))\), where _f_ is any computable function. Note that we do not need to allow a separate polynomial dependence on \(\ell\) as for all non-trivial instances \(\ell\le N\).

Observation B.1. \((\ell,d)\)_-CMM is W\[1\]-hard by d for both f<sub>E</sub> and_ \(f_{\chi^2}\).

_Proof._ The result follows by checking that the reduction from \[1\] is a parameterized reduction from balanced biclique, parameterized by solution size, to \((\ell,d)\)-CMM parameterized by _d_.

An outline of the reduction strategy is as follows. The reduction takes a graph as input and produces a node-labeled graph such that a motif consisting of 0s and _d_ wildcards selects exactly the _d_ nodes at its wildcard positions, so every set of _d_ nodes can be selected (a motif containing a 1 selects at most one node). A motif pair selecting two disjoint sets of _d_ nodes each maximizes the support function if and only if the selected subgraph is a biclique. Thus finding a motif pair with _d_ wildcards and the best possible support value is equivalent to finding a biclique _K<sub>d,d</sub>_, a problem that is known to be W\[1\]-hard by solution size \[19\]. \(\sqcap\sqcup\)

In fact, the authors of \[1\] show NP-hardness for an even larger class of support functions (which they call _compliant biclique-maximal_ support functions). We omit that discussion, because it is quite technical, and refer the interested reader to \[1\].
